titleStmt.title: Mice and rats achieve similar levels of performance in an adaptive decision-making task
titleStmt.author: Jaramillo
Zador

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Mice and rats achieve similar levels of performance in an adaptive decision-making task

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether mice can perform an adaptive decision-making task as well as rats, the established rodent model for it
span.quote: Two opposing constraints exist when choosing a model organism for studying the neural basis of adaptive decision-making: (1) experimental access and (2) behavioral complexity. Available molecular and genetic approaches for studying neural circuits in the mouse fulfill the first requirement. In contrast, it is still under debate if mice can perform cognitive tasks of sufficient complexity.

span.label: how learning speed, performance level and speed of adaptation compare between the two species on one flexible categorization task
span.quote: However, mice offer further advantages over rats, stemming mainly from the availability of hundreds of transgenic lines that enable precise targeting of gene expression to defined neuronal populations (Madisen et al., 2010 ; Taniguchi et al., 2011 ; Madisen et al., 2012 ; Gerfen et al., 2013 ). It is therefore crucial to evaluate whether mice can achieve the high levels of performance on cognitive tasks that has previously been demonstrated in rats.

span.label: shows mice reach the same performance and adapt as fast as rats though they take longer to learn, and argues the residual learning gap may be an artefact of using a task built for rats
span.quote: We found that both species achieved similarly high performance levels. On average, rats learned the task faster than mice, although some mice were as fast as the average rat. No major differences in subjective categorization boundaries or the speed of adaptation between the two species were found.

span.label: null-result
span.quote: No major differences in subjective categorization boundaries or the speed of adaptation between the two species were found.

span.label: adaptive decision-making in rodents
span.quote: The task required animals to categorize acoustic stimuli as high- or low-frequency sounds, and to adapt quickly after changes in the category boundary.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Here we compare learning and performance of mice and rats, the preferred behavioral rodent model, during an acoustic flexible categorization two-alternative choice task.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: behavioural adaptation is modelled as an internal category boundary that shifts between blocks, which is why the change generalises to untrained frequencies rather than being limited to the reversing tone
span.quote: the observation that animals generalize to other frequencies is well captured by a model in which an internal category boundary shifts between blocks of trials

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: two candidate physiological routes to the same behavioural switch: synaptic-weight change in the sensory-motor pathway (learning/memory), or on-line integration of sensory and context information without lasting synaptic change (selective attention)
span.quote: Similarly, there are at least two possible mechanisms for this adaptation in behavior: (1) changes in synaptic strength in the sensory-motor pathway that result in different behavioral responses for the same sound; or (2) integration of sensory and context information without long-term synaptic changes in the sensory-motor pathway.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: measured rat superiority may be produced by the tasks themselves, since comparisons use paradigms originally engineered around rat ethology
span.quote: This potential confound may explain why rats have been found to be better in a variety of tasks

span.label: animals could be tracking the outcome of the reversing 7 kHz tone, or using the extreme tones as a cue to which contingency is active, and the paper allows both
span.quote: Animals could use various strategies for solving the task described in this study. First, animals may evaluate the outcome of responses to the reversing frequency (7 kHz) to update their sound-action associations. Alternatively, the appearance of an extreme stimulus (3 or 16.3 kHz) could be used as a cue indicating the most likely contingency. These strategies are non-exclusive, and animals may be taking advantage of both.

span.label: the adaptation could be synaptic change in the sensory-motor pathway or context integration without lasting change - learning or attention
span.quote: Similarly, there are at least two possible mechanisms for this adaptation in behavior: (1) changes in synaptic strength in the sensory-motor pathway that result in different behavioral responses for the same sound; or (2) integration of sensory and context information without long-term synaptic changes in the sensory-motor pathway. The former correspond to mechanisms hypothesized for learning and memory (Martin et al., 2000 ), the latter to mechanisms of selective attention (Jaramillo and Pearlmutter, 2007 ), both defining features of cognition.

span.label: whatever the strategy, the generalisation across untrained frequencies is captured by an internal boundary that shifts between blocks
span.quote: Animals could use various strategies for solving the task described in this study. First, animals may evaluate the outcome of responses to the reversing frequency (7 kHz) to update their sound-action associations. Alternatively, the appearance of an extreme stimulus (3 or 16.3 kHz) could be used as a cue indicating the most likely contingency. These strategies are non-exclusive, and animals may be taking advantage of both.

span.label: The comparison uses a task originally designed for rats, a confound that may bias species comparisons in the rat's favour.
span.quote: Most comparisons of behavioral performance between mice and rats, including our study, have used tasks originally devised for rats.

span.label: Behavioural data alone cannot distinguish the candidate mechanisms (synaptic change in the sensory-motor pathway versus contextual integration without such change) underlying the adaptation.
span.quote: Although behavioral measurements alone may not dissociate between these possibilities, techniques for physiological analysis of neural circuits in the mouse have the potential to reveal the mechanisms that mediate this rapid adaptation in the interpretation of sounds.

span.label: Training parameters were held constant to permit a species comparison, so the reported training times are not optimized and would differ under individually tuned protocols.
span.quote: Other objectives, for example minimizing training times for each animal, may require adjusting parameters for each individual.

span.label: the paper names a confound that undercuts its own headline result: the task was devised for rats, which may be why rats look faster
span.quote: Most comparisons of behavioral performance between mice and rats, including our study, have used tasks originally devised for rats. This potential confound may explain why rats have been found to be better in a variety of tasks

span.label: behaviour alone cannot separate the learning account from the attention account of the adaptation
span.quote: Although behavioral measurements alone may not dissociate between these possibilities, techniques for physiological analysis of neural circuits in the mouse have the potential to reveal the mechanisms that mediate this rapid adaptation in the interpretation of sounds.

span.label: one mouse never learned the discrimination and one rat never reached the final stage; both were dropped
span.quote: One mouse never learned the discrimination task, although this animal showed no impairment in initiating trials or collecting reward. One rat never reached the final stage (7-OK). These animals were excluded from subsequent analysis.

span.label: training was set for comparability rather than for each animal's best performance, so the levels reported are not ceilings
span.quote: In this study, we set the duration of behavioral sessions to 1 h for all stages of training, kept the amount of reward per trial constant, and used the same criteria to advanced each individual from one stage to the next. Consistency in training parameters helped us compare directly the two species, the main goal of the study. Other objectives, for example minimizing training times for each animal, may require adjusting parameters for each individual.

span.label: the C57Bl/6J strain loses hearing with age, which had to be checked separately before auditory results could be trusted
span.quote: An important consideration when working with mice is that some strains suffer from early loss of hearing sensitivity (Zheng et al., 1999 ). C57Bl/6J, a common background for transgenics used in the study of neural circuits, show elevated auditory brainstem response thresholds at 700 days of age (60 dB higher than normal), but not at 200 days of age.

span.label: the two-alternative forced choice psychophysical paradigm, brought down to rodents
span.quote: Smaller mammals, rodents in particular, provide several advantages over primates for physiological experiments: faster breeding times, lower costs, smaller housing needs, and currently, easier access to molecular and genetic tools.

span.label: the fitted logistic and its two parameters, boundary and slope, as the description of a subject's categorisation
span.quote: We then fitted a logistic function to the psychometric performance and evaluated two parameters: the subjective category boundary and the slope of the curve.

span.label: the same task across species is an EQUIVALENCE CLAIM resting on declared adjustments: reward volume scaled to each species' normal consumption, tubing gauge changed, sound levels set above each species' own threshold
span.quote: The volume of water reward was scaled according to the normal consumption for each species

span.label: similar performance here means failure to reject a difference at n=10 per species, not a demonstrated equivalence - the paper's own phrasing is that no major differences were found
span.quote: We found that both species achieved similarly high performance levels. On average, rats learned the task faster than mice, although some mice were as fast as the average rat. No major differences in subjective categorization boundaries or the speed of adaptation between the two species were found.

span.label: subjective category boundary is the 50% point of a fitted logistic, distinct from the experimenter's boundary, and it is what shifts between blocks
span.quote: We then fitted a logistic function to the psychometric performance and evaluated two parameters: the subjective category boundary and the slope of the curve.

span.label: speed of switching is measured as the trial at which an exponential fit crosses chance, not as trials to criterion
span.quote: We estimated the speed of switching to a new sound-action association by averaging performance for each trial from several sessions, and calculating when an exponential fit crossed the 50% chance performance level

span.label: valid trials exclude early withdrawals, so every performance figure is conditioned on the animal having waited out the sound
span.quote: If animals withdrew before the end of the stimulus, the trial was aborted and denoted as invalid. Only valid trials were used in calculations of the fraction of correct trials.

span.label: builds-on → Jaramillo et al. (2014), the flexible sound-categorization task and shifting-boundary model
span.quote: Here we compare the speed of learning and the performance levels achieved by mice and rats in a decision-making task that tested the animals' perceptual abilities as well as their adaptability (Jaramillo et al., 2014 ).

span.label: confirms → vibrotactile comparisons finding mice and rats similar on psychometric curves, reaction times and learning rates
span.quote: In a two-alternative forced choice paradigm for vibrotactile discrimination, the performance of mice and rats was found to be very similar when quantifying psychometric curves, reaction times, learning rates, and trial omissions

span.label: qualifies → the body of comparisons in which rats outperform mice, by identifying the rat-derived task as a shared confound
span.quote: Most comparisons of behavioral performance between mice and rats, including our study, have used tasks originally devised for rats. This potential confound may explain why rats have been found to be better in a variety of tasks

span.label: critiques → the assumption that a paradigm can be carried over from rat to mouse unchanged
span.quote: Successful behavioral paradigms, however, rely on targeting designs to the idiosyncrasies of the mouse from the outset, rather than simply assuming that mice are little rats.

span.label: supports → the reinterpretation of water-maze species differences as swimming differences rather than memory differences
span.quote: Behavior of the two species was similar in the navigation tasks when evaluated in the dry-land maze. Differences found in water-maze tasks seem to be accounted for mostly by differences in swimming rather than memory capabilities.

span.label: extends → rodent psychophysics paradigms modelled on primate decision-making tasks
span.quote: Smaller mammals, rodents in particular, provide several advantages over primates for physiological experiments: faster breeding times, lower costs, smaller housing needs, and currently, easier access to molecular and genetic tools.

span.label: subjective category boundary —operationalised-as→ psychometric
span.quote: We then fitted a logistic function to the psychometric performance and evaluated two parameters: the subjective category boundary and the slope of the curve.

span.label: flexible categorization —operationalised-as→ contingency
span.quote: The categorization contingency changed from one block to the next without any additional cue indicating the change (besides the sound-action-reward relations). The initial contingency for each session was alternated from one day to the next.

span.label: mice —contrasted-with→ rats
span.quote: We found that rats learned the basic discrimination task (reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks) faster than mice ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test). On average, rats reached the criterion of 80% correct for all stimuli by session 9.8 ± 0.9 (mean ± SD ), while mice took 18.1 ± 4.2 sessions.

span.label: mice —part-of→ transgenic lines
span.quote: However, mice offer further advantages over rats, stemming mainly from the availability of hundreds of transgenic lines that enable precise targeting of gene expression to defined neuronal populations (Madisen et al., 2010 ; Taniguchi et al., 2011 ; Madisen et al., 2012 ; Gerfen et al., 2013 ). It is therefore crucial to evaluate whether mice can achieve the high levels of performance on cognitive tasks that has previously been demonstrated in rats.

span.label: ethological validity —distinct-from→ flexible categorization
span.quote: Most comparisons of behavioral performance between mice and rats, including our study, have used tasks originally devised for rats. This potential confound may explain why rats have been found to be better in a variety of tasks

span.label: selective attention —contrasted-with→ learning and memory
span.quote: Similarly, there are at least two possible mechanisms for this adaptation in behavior: (1) changes in synaptic strength in the sensory-motor pathway that result in different behavioral responses for the same sound; or (2) integration of sensory and context information without long-term synaptic changes in the sensory-motor pathway. The former correspond to mechanisms hypothesized for learning and memory (Martin et al., 2000 ), the latter to mechanisms of selective attention (Jaramillo and Pearlmutter, 2007 ), both defining features of cognition.

span.label: valid trials —distinct-from→ early withdrawals
span.quote: If animals withdrew before the end of the stimulus, the trial was aborted and denoted as invalid. Only valid trials were used in calculations of the fraction of correct trials.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · bias-correction —causes→ chance level
span.quote: Note that for an average of 500 trials per session, performance below 56% would be considered at chance ( p < 0.01, binomial test), as indicated by the dotted lines in Figure 3

span.label: training stages —part-of→ flexible categorization
span.quote: Training parameters (session duration, reward amount, etc.) were set to make conditions as similar as possible for all individuals and across the two species, instead of trying to minimize the training time or maximize performance for each individual.

span.label: bias-correction —causes→ chance level
span.quote: In contrast, mice were either at chance level or had the bias-correction mode activated, resulting in performances below chance.

span.label: Wilcoxon rank-sum test
span.quote: We found that rats learned the basic discrimination task (reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks) faster than mice ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test).

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Animals received free water on weekends resulting in a clear difference between the number of trials on the first day of the week and subsequent days for both species ( p = 0.0077, for rats and for mice, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

span.label: Spearman correlation
span.quote: There was no apparent correlation between the trials required to complete stages 5-RC (Required Correct) and 6-SB (Switch in Blocks) for either mice or rats (|ρ| < 0.12, p = 0.57, Spearman correlation).

span.label: binomial test
span.quote: Note that for an average of 500 trials per session, performance below 56% would be considered at chance ( p < 0.01, binomial test)

span.label: maximum likelihood fitting of a logistic psychometric function
span.term: maximum likelihood fitting of a logistic psychometric function
span.quote: Briefly, a constrained maximum likelihood method was used to fit a logistic function with 4 parameters: α (the 50% threshold, or boundary), 1/β (the slope of the curve), γ (the lower asymptote), and λ (the higher asymptote).

span.label: nonlinear curve fitting
span.quote: we fit an exponential function to the performance in response to the reversing stimulus after a contingency switch

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: Error bars are 95% confidence intervals.

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Error bars correspond to standard deviations.

span.label: rank-sum test
span.quote: We found that rats learned the basic discrimination task (reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks) faster than mice ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test). On average, rats reached the criterion of 80% correct for all stimuli by session 9.8 ± 0.9 (mean ± SD ), while mice took 18.1 ± 4.2 sessions.

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Animals received free water on weekends resulting in a clear difference between the number of trials on the first day of the week and subsequent days for both species ( p = 0.0077, for rats and for mice, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

span.label: Spearman correlation
span.quote: There was no apparent correlation between the trials required to complete stages 5-RC (Required Correct) and 6-SB (Switch in Blocks) for either mice or rats (|ρ| < 0.12, p = 0.57, Spearman correlation).

span.label: binomial test
span.quote: Note that for an average of 500 trials per session, performance below 56% would be considered at chance ( p < 0.01, binomial test), as indicated by the dotted lines in Figure 3

span.label: logistic function
span.quote: We then fitted a logistic function to the psychometric performance and evaluated two parameters: the subjective category boundary and the slope of the curve.

span.label: Rats reached the basic sound-discrimination criterion in significantly fewer sessions than mice.
span.quote: We found that rats learned the basic discrimination task (reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks) faster than mice ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test).

span.label: Despite the difference in learning speed, the two species converged on comparably high asymptotic performance.
span.quote: We found that both species achieved similarly high performance levels.

span.label: Nearly all of the species difference in total training length came from the single stage in which animals learned the sound discrimination itself.
span.quote: From all stages, stage 5-RC (Required Correct), in which animals learned to discriminate sounds, showed the largest difference between mice and rats (7 sessions on average, p = 0.0003, rank-sum test).

span.label: Once trained, mice and rats re-adapted to a reversed category boundary at the same speed, needing roughly ten trials.
span.quote: We found that both rats and mice needed about 10 trials to switch between contingencies (Figure 5E , p = 0.72, rank-sum test).

span.label: The size of the shift in subjective category boundary between contingencies did not differ between species, although mice had slightly steeper psychometric slopes.
span.quote: The change in subjective category boundary as animals switched from one contingency to the other was not different between mice and rats ( p = 0.89 rank-sum test), but mice showed slightly steeper slopes than rats ( p = 0.019 on the low-boundary block, p < 0.001 on the high-boundary block).

span.label: Age-related hearing loss in the C57Bl/6J strain did not prevent mice from performing the auditory task over several hundred days.
span.quote: We found that C57Bl/6J mice can perform the auditory flexible categorization task for several hundred days without major impairments in performance.

span.label: rats reached the switching stage in 9.8 sessions on average against 18.1 for mice
span.quote: We found that rats learned the basic discrimination task (reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks) faster than mice ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test). On average, rats reached the criterion of 80% correct for all stimuli by session 9.8 ± 0.9 (mean ± SD ), while mice took 18.1 ± 4.2 sessions.

span.label: the gap was concentrated in the discrimination stage, about seven sessions of it
span.quote: From all stages, stage 5-RC (Required Correct), in which animals learned to discriminate sounds, showed the largest difference between mice and rats (7 sessions on average, p = 0.0003, rank-sum test). This stage was responsible for most of the difference in the overall length of training.

span.label: the distributions overlapped and some mice matched the average rat
span.quote: Overall, rats reached the final stage (7-OK) faster than mice (Figure 2G ) ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test), although the distributions largely overlapped and some mice were as fast as the average rat.

span.label: mice ended slightly ahead on overall performance and had steeper psychometric slopes
span.quote: Although both species achieved a similar fraction of correct trials per session (Figure 3C ), mice showed a slightly higher average performance on the last stages ( p < 0.05 rank-sum test, for several consecutive sessions after reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks).

span.label: nine of ten animals in each species exceeded 70% on the reversing tone in both contingencies
span.quote: Nine out of ten animals from each species achieved performance levels above 70% for this reversing stimulus on both contingencies (Figure 2 ). Performance for the non-reversing stimuli (3 and 16.3 kHz) was always above this level.

span.label: hearing loss in the C57Bl/6J strain did not impair the task even past 300 days of age
span.quote: We found that C57Bl/6J mice can perform the auditory flexible categorization task for several hundred days without major impairments in performance.

span.label: CONTROL NULL: both species took about ten trials to switch contingency, with no species difference
span.quote: We found that both rats and mice needed about 10 trials to switch between contingencies (Figure 5E , p = 0.72, rank-sum test).

span.label: CONTROL NULL: the shift in subjective category boundary between contingencies did not differ between species
span.quote: The change in subjective category boundary as animals switched from one contingency to the other was not different between mice and rats ( p = 0.89 rank-sum test), but mice showed slightly steeper slopes than rats ( p = 0.019 on the low-boundary block, p < 0.001 on the high-boundary block).

span.label: CONTROL NULL: trials completed per session did not differ reliably, though mice varied more
span.quote: We found no statistically reliable difference in the average number of trials per session between mice and rats for the reward amounts used in our study ( p = 0.12, rank-sum test), although the variability across animals was larger in the cohort of mice

span.label: CONTROL NULL: early withdrawals were about 20% in both species
span.quote: Early withdrawals were about 20% on average for both mice and rats ( p = 0.56, rank-sum test), although variability was higher for mice. Analysis of subsequent sessions showed that the average for rats remained in the range 15–20%, while the average for mice fluctuated in the range 20–30%.

span.label: CONTROL NULL: trials needed to learn discrimination did not predict trials needed to learn switching, in either species
span.quote: There was no apparent correlation between the trials required to complete stages 5-RC (Required Correct) and 6-SB (Switch in Blocks) for either mice or rats (|ρ| < 0.12, p = 0.57, Spearman correlation).

span.label: CONTROL: a side-bias or alternation strategy would have scored under 60% in essentially every session
span.quote: Post-hoc analysis of the trials presented in each session verified that a strategy of always choosing one side, would yield performances below 60% on 98% of the sessions. Similarly, a strategy of alternating sides would yield performances below 60% on 99.9% of the sessions.

span.label: both species ran fewer trials on the first day back after free water at the weekend
span.quote: Animals received free water on weekends resulting in a clear difference between the number of trials on the first day of the week and subsequent days for both species ( p = 0.0077, for rats and for mice, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).

span.label: invalid trial
span.quote: If animals withdrew before the end of the stimulus, the trial was aborted and denoted as invalid.

span.label: reversing vs non-reversing stimuli
span.quote: Previous studies from our group showed that performance for reversing stimuli (in this case, 7 kHz) is lower than for non-reversing stimuli (3 and 16.3 kHz)

span.label: number of trials to switch
span.quote: The number of trials to switch was calculated as the point at which the exponential fit crossed the 50% chance level performance.

span.label: flexible categorization
span.quote: After a series of training stages described in the next section, animals were required to perform a frequency discrimination task in which the boundary that separated high- from low-frequency sounds varied within a session.

span.label: valid trials
span.quote: If animals withdrew before the end of the stimulus, the trial was aborted and denoted as invalid. Only valid trials were used in calculations of the fraction of correct trials.

span.label: subjective category boundary
span.quote: We then fitted a logistic function to the psychometric performance and evaluated two parameters: the subjective category boundary and the slope of the curve.

span.label: chance level
span.quote: Note that for an average of 500 trials per session, performance below 56% would be considered at chance ( p < 0.01, binomial test), as indicated by the dotted lines in Figure 3

span.label: ethological validity
span.quote: Behavioral paradigms for mice should therefore be designed taking into account the ethological validity of the task requirements. Small changes in the training apparatus and protocols can make a difference. For instance, previous measurements in our lab indicated that rats may not need the first stage of training (1-DS) presented in this study, but mice benefit greatly from this conditioning stage.

span.label: species (mouse vs rat)
span.quote: Here we compare learning and performance of mice and rats, the preferred behavioral rodent model, during an acoustic flexible categorization two-alternative choice task.

span.label: categorization contingency (uncued block-wise switch of the category boundary)
span.term: categorization contingency (uncued block-wise switch of the category boundary)
span.quote: The categorization contingency changed from one block to the next without any additional cue indicating the change

span.label: number of sessions/trials needed to pass each training stage
span.term: number of sessions/trials needed to pass each training stage
span.quote: We quantified how many sessions were needed on each stage for animals to successfully learn the task

span.label: fraction of correct trials
span.quote: Only valid trials were used in calculations of the fraction of correct trials.

span.label: subjective category boundary and psychometric slope
span.term: subjective category boundary and psychometric slope
span.quote: We then fitted a logistic function to the psychometric performance and evaluated two parameters: the subjective category boundary and the slope of the curve.

span.label: session duration, reward per trial and advancement criteria (held constant across individuals and species)
span.term: session duration, reward per trial and advancement criteria (held constant across individuals and species)
span.quote: In this study, we set the duration of behavioral sessions to 1 h for all stages of training, kept the amount of reward per trial constant, and used the same criteria to advanced each individual from one stage to the next.

span.label: sound intensity (roved to block a loudness cue)
span.term: sound intensity (roved to block a loudness cue)
span.quote: The intensity of the sounds was variable in the range 50–70 dB-SPL to discourage the use of loudness to solve the task

span.label: training stages
span.quote: We found that rats learned the basic discrimination task (reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks) faster than mice ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test). On average, rats reached the criterion of 80% correct for all stimuli by session 9.8 ± 0.9 (mean ± SD ), while mice took 18.1 ± 4.2 sessions.

span.label: subjective category boundary
span.quote: The change in subjective category boundary as animals switched from one contingency to the other was not different between mice and rats ( p = 0.89 rank-sum test), but mice showed slightly steeper slopes than rats ( p = 0.019 on the low-boundary block, p < 0.001 on the high-boundary block).

span.label: slope
span.quote: Although both species achieved a similar fraction of correct trials per session (Figure 3C ), mice showed a slightly higher average performance on the last stages ( p < 0.05 rank-sum test, for several consecutive sessions after reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks).

span.label: early withdrawals
span.quote: Early withdrawals were about 20% on average for both mice and rats ( p = 0.56, rank-sum test), although variability was higher for mice. Analysis of subsequent sessions showed that the average for rats remained in the range 15–20%, while the average for mice fluctuated in the range 20–30%.

span.label: 9.8 ± 0.9 — mean number of sessions rats needed to reach the 80%-correct criterion (mice needed 18.1 ± 4.2)
span.quote: On average, rats reached the criterion of 80% correct for all stimuli by session 9.8 ± 0.9

span.label: 2320 — average number of trials by which rats beat mice on the discrimination-learning stage
span.quote: Stage 5-RC (Required Correct), showed the largest difference between species (rats required 2320 fewer trials on average, p = 0.0013, rank-sum test).

span.label: about 10 trials — trials needed by both species to cross chance performance again after a contingency switch
span.quote: We found that both rats and mice needed about 10 trials to switch between contingencies (Figure 5E , p = 0.72, rank-sum test).

span.label: about 20% — share of trials with early withdrawal from the centre port, statistically indistinguishable between species
span.quote: Early withdrawals were about 20% on average for both mice and rats ( p = 0.56, rank-sum test), although variability was higher for mice.

span.label: ten and ten — cohort sizes: ten Long Evans rats and ten C57Bl/6J mice
span.quote: Ten adult male Long Evans rats (Taconic Farms) and ten adult male C57Bl/6J mice (The Jackson Laboratory, stock #000664) were used in this study

span.label: 56% — performance level below which a 500-trial session counts as chance
span.quote: Note that for an average of 500 trials per session, performance below 56% would be considered at chance ( p < 0.01, binomial test)

span.label: 9.8 vs 18.1 sessions — sessions to reach the switching stage, rats against mice
span.quote: We found that rats learned the basic discrimination task (reaching stage 6-SB, Switch in Blocks) faster than mice ( p = 0.0014, rank-sum test). On average, rats reached the criterion of 80% correct for all stimuli by session 9.8 ± 0.9 (mean ± SD ), while mice took 18.1 ± 4.2 sessions.

span.label: about 10 trials — trials to recover chance performance after an uncued contingency switch, in both species
span.quote: We found that both rats and mice needed about 10 trials to switch between contingencies (Figure 5E , p = 0.72, rank-sum test).

span.label: 24 ul vs 2-3 ul — reward per trial, scaled to each species' normal consumption - the adjustment that makes the task comparable
span.quote: The volume of water reward was scaled according to the normal consumption for each species

span.label: 0-20 dB-SPL vs 10-40 dB-SPL — hearing thresholds of rats against mice over the frequencies used
span.quote: Although rats and mice have different absolute thresholds for the frequencies used here: 0–20 dB-SPL for rats (Heffner et al., 1994 ) and 10–40 dB-SPL for mice (Koay et al., 2002 ), all sounds were presented above threshold for either species.

span.label: 300 — valid trials per block before the categorisation boundary reversed
span.quote: A single session (1 h) consisted of several blocks of 300 valid trials.

span.label: 56% — the chance ceiling for a 500-trial session by binomial test
span.quote: Note that for an average of 500 trials per session, performance below 56% would be considered at chance ( p < 0.01, binomial test), as indicated by the dotted lines in Figure 3

span.label: 50-70 dB-SPL — roving sound level, used so loudness cannot solve the task
span.quote: The intensity of the sounds was variable in the range 50–70 dB-SPL to discourage the use of loudness to solve the task; the perceived loudness of a sound depends on frequency even when the same sound-pressure level reaches the ear.
